USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain the current tariff posture already in place (25% on ~$34B, with the ~$200B threat held as leverage) but do not push the escalation further — hold off on raising the List 3 rate to 25% and keep the door open to talks. The US is in a strong macro position and holds the leverage, so this is not a moment to concede or roll back; but neither is it a moment to deepen a fight where China has refused to blink and retaliation is already aimed at the American farm belt.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is mild-positive (+0.2), not existential, because the American economy is demonstrably strong entering this: the broad dollar is up ~7% over the window (107.6 to 115.2), industrial production is rising (102.2 to 104.0), and CPI is moderate — so the dispute is nowhere near a material GDP/recession anchor. The threat is real but limited and centered on second-order political/economic costs: the July 6 $34B tariffs are live, an additional ~$200B is proposed and being considered at 25% (Aug 1), and China responded Aug 3 with a ~$60B retaliation list targeting agricultural goods (soybeans, honey, meat) that directly pressure Trump's 2016 rural base, while Michigan consumer sentiment has slipped from 101.4 to 96.2 and Republican leaders (e.g. Senate Finance Chairman Hatch) and business groups are already alarmed at further escalation. The action stance is hold (0.0) rather than escalate because escalating to $200B/25% would trigger the promised $60B retaliation, deepen a deadlock in which both sides report no settlement in sight, and hand the farm-belt constituencies a concrete cost right before midterms — while the dollar's strength and the fact that China is running out of goods to tax (only ~$120B left to retaliate after the $34B round) means the US loses little by letting the existing pressure sit and signaling willingness to negotiate. This is the disciplined midpoint: no new commitments (not concede/purchase), no new escalation (not retaliate/escalate).
key_factors: US macro strength entering the dispute: broad dollar +~7%, industrial production rising, moderate CPI
Escalation already in force: 25% tariffs on ~$34B (July 6) with ~$200B proposed and considered at 25% (Aug 1)
China retaliating and refusing to blink: ~$60B retaliation list (Aug 3) targeting farm-belt goods (soybeans, honey, meat)
Consumer sentiment drifting down (Michigan 101.4 to 96.2) and Republican/business opposition to further escalation
US leverage: large bilateral deficit and China running low on goods available to tax gives the US room to hold pressure
Pending decision point: $200B public hearings Aug 20-23, decision after Aug 30

sources_cited.excerpt: List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines).
USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
China announced it would hit about $60B of US exports with new tariffs in response to Trump's decision to escalate potential trade penalties
Administration officials said the tariff fight is aimed at forcing China to change; China only bought about $135B in US goods last year, so it will run out of American products to tax

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold current posture — do not escalate into new retaliation, do not capitulate on structural tech/IP issues. Keep the existing in-kind tariff retaliation in place as credible deterrence, defend the yuan and domestic economy via the FX toolkit and RRR liquidity support, and keep a negotiating channel open so the onus for further escalation stays on Washington rather than Beijing.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not yet existential. The US has already imposed 25% tariffs on ~$34B (live July 6), finalized ~$16B more (effective Aug 23), and proposed a ~$200B List 3 that USTR is considering raising from 10% to 25% (Aug 1) — together covering roughly half of all US-China trade. This directly threatens China's export economy and tech/ICT sector, evidenced by the ZTE denial order (April 16). Macro pressure is visible: the yuan fell >7% since April and crossed 6.9 in early August, forcing the PBOC to reinstate the forward-FX reserve requirement and cut the RRR to support liquidity. Crucially, China's retaliation capacity is structurally asymmetric (US imports ~$500B from China vs. much smaller reverse flows), so an escalation war is one China cannot win on dollar terms and the US has explicitly conditioned the $200B/25% move on Chinese retaliation — escalating would hand Washington the exact pretext it wants and inflict far more damage than any asymmetric retort could. Yet the threat is not yet existential: List 3 is still in the comment phase (hearing Aug 20-23), the ~$34B already effective is a small share of China's exports, and China retains large FX reserves and capital controls to buffer financial stress. Hence +0.6, not +1.0. The action stance (0.0, hold) reflects that maximal escalation is the losing move here (it triggers the broader $200B/25% cascade and a vicious capital-outflow cycle), while any conceding posture would sacrifice core industrial-policy and IP positions tied to CCP legitimacy and tech-autonomy goals — premature and domestically untenable. Holding firm with calibrated deterrence and staying open to a negotiated settlement maximizes leverage over US farm-belt/consumer constituencies without walking into the escalation trap.
key_factors: US List 3 (~$200B) proposed, rate possibly 25% per Aug 1 — would cover ~half of US-China trade
List 1 (25% on ~$34B) live July 6; List 2 (~$16B) effective Aug 23
Yuan down >7% since April, ~6.9/USD in early Aug; PBOC reinstated forward-FX reserve rule + RRR cut
China retaliation capacity asymmetric vs US import coverage — escalation spiral favors the US
ZTE denial order (Apr 16) shows firm-level tech/ICT vulnerability
List 3 still in comment/hearing phase — not yet imposed, so not existential
